title: Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–11)
hook: a hard story about lying to the community
carry: the bible keeps the hard stories

segments.voice: Yesterday, two ordinary men before the council. Your line was they had been with Jesus. What did you tell someone you'd seen? Day five hundred thirty-nine.

Founding stories tend to get polished. The brochure keeps the triumphs and quietly drops the rest. Which makes this part of Acts surprising. Luke has just described the first Christians in Jerusalem as one heart and one soul, sharing everything, so that no one among them was in need. A man named Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet. And then, right after that glowing picture, Luke tells a story that is very hard to read.
screen: `THE STORY LEFT OUT.` → `ONE HEART AND ONE SOUL.` → `THEN, A HARD STORY.`

segments.voice: A married couple, Ananias and Sapphira, sell a piece of land too. They keep back part of the money and bring the rest, presenting it as the whole. Nobody required them to sell, or to give it all. Peter says so: while it remained, was it not yours? And after it was sold, wasn't the money in your power? The problem isn't the amount. It's the pretending. Peter tells Ananias: "Thou hast not lied to men, but to God." And Ananias falls down and dies. About three hours later Sapphira comes in, not knowing what has happened. Peter asks her straight: did you sell the land for so much? She says yes, for so much. And she falls down and dies too. Luke says great fear came upon the whole church: the Greek word is ekklēsia, the assembly. What do we do with a story like this? The text doesn't explain how they died or say anything about their eternal fate. Some readers see God's judgment; others see a shock so great it killed them; the passage itself doesn't settle it. What it does say is that a community built on sharing can be poisoned by pretending, by people performing generosity they don't have. And Luke didn't leave it out. The founding story of the Church includes this, and Peter's denial, and the disciples' squabbles. That's week seventy-seven: feed my sheep, witness, Matthias, Peter's first sermon, silver and gold, we cannot but speak, and a hard story. The Bible keeps the hard stories.
screen: `ONE HEART, THEN A PRETENSE.` · `NOT THE AMOUNT: THE PRETENDING.` · `THE FIRST CHURCH, IN FEAR.` · `LUKE DIDN'T LEAVE IT OUT.` · then, large: `ANANIAS AND SAPPHIRA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one place where you're pretending. Sit and breathe. It can be small: saying fine when it isn't, letting people think you did more than you did, a number rounded up, a story improved. Let one come to mind. No punishment, just honesty. Picture what it would look like to set the record straight, or simply to stop adding to it. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is, or think of it in light of the sacrament of confession. If you don't, just see it clearly. The bell holds the time.
Ekklēsia. Luke's word for the assembly of believers, seized by fear after Ananias and Sapphira's pretense was exposed. Today's word.
Your line: the bible keeps the hard stories. Today, be honest about one thing you'd usually polish, even something small. Day five hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics examine their conscience, often at night, and confess serious sins in the sacrament of penance; the early community's sharing in Acts 4 and 5 is read at Mass in the Easter season.

fork.setup: you're Sapphira. three hours after your husband, you walk in. Peter asks, did you sell the land for so much? what do you say?
options: tell the truth: we kept part back.
fork.reveal: she repeats the lie: yea, for so much. and she falls down too. Peter gave her the chance to tell the truth.

original.note: Greek: church, assembly. Luke's word at 5:11 for the believers seized by fear.

trapdoor: what you thought: God strikes down people who don't give enough.
what it means: giving was free; the deadly thing was pretending, inside a community built on trust.
what a scholar hears: 'kept back' (nosphizomai) is the verb the Greek Old Testament uses for Achan's theft (Joshua 7:1); 5:11 is the first use of ekklēsia in Acts in the critical text.

sources.quoted: Thou hast not lied to men, but to God.

notes: Interpretations of the deaths are presented as differing readings without endorsing one. Keeper to confirm.
Nosphizomai in Acts 5:2–3 and LXX Joshua 7:1 (Achan). Confirm.
Ekklēsia first in Acts at 5:11 in the critical text (the textus receptus has it at 2:47). Confirm.
